title: How To Reach Students Who’ve Shut Down
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin describes an increase in withdrawn students — refusing to work, barely speaking, hiding behind hoodies — and argues that the typical adult response of direct questions and escalating threats only drives them further inward. His alternative is a slow, patient rapport-building process built entirely on small, low-pressure gestures: a smile, a quiet hello, a fist bump, repeated consistently and without any agenda attached. He stresses that questions about the student's wellbeing, motivation, or work must be avoided entirely during this phase, since withdrawn students can detect insincerity immediately and any hint of an ulterior motive collapses the fragile trust being built. Only once genuine rapport is firmly established, he says, can a teacher gently circle back to assessing needs or offering help. The piece frames this as a long game requiring patience, but one that reliably works because it removes the pressure that caused the student to shut down in the first place.
points: Direct questions and escalating threats toward withdrawn students typically push them further into isolation rather than reaching them.
Rapport with a shut-down student must be built through small, low-pressure gestures — a smile, a quiet hello, a fist bump — with no agenda attached.
Withdrawn students can detect insincerity immediately, so any hint of an ulterior motive during rapport-building will collapse trust.
Only after genuine rapport is firmly established should a teacher circle back to gently assess needs or offer help.
A student's mental health takes priority over academics during this process, and the student must be allowed to set the pace.
quotes: But the way most teachers (and counselors) engage these struggling students makes reaching them all the more difficult.
The questions and threats only push students deeper into themselves and all but ensure they’ll never emerge from their shell.
It’s little by little, and starting as small as a fleck of dust, to build a trusting relationship with the student. It can be a brief smile. It can be a low-key hello.
No questions. No threats. No flattery, fakery, or cajolement. No talk of motivation or work habits or even school. There can never be strings attached.
And be forewarned: They can recognize a phony from a mile away.
